source: Taylor (2020) Folk physics for crows? Animal Behavior and Cognition 7(3):452-456
finding: Baseline for the whole subfield. Of six New Caledonian crows, three learned the trap-tube, passed obvious-feature removal, the inverted tube and the trap-table. They then failed a two-hole tube where only one hole had a base. Author reads this as: the crows knew the hole-food link, but not the unseen cause (gravity).
numbers: 3 of 6 crows learned the initial trap-tube; all 3 passed inverted-tube and trap-table; all failed the two-hole transfer (only one hole had a base).
quote: the crows had knowledge of the meat's relation with the hole as a proximate causal regularity but did not infer the existence of a distal causal mechanism
limits: Small sample (3 successful birds). Author calls the whole conclusion premature; also, the step from observable cues to unobservable mechanism is a big jump in task difficulty.
agent_relevance: Passing a transfer test does not show the agent holds the deep rule. Add a probe where the surface cue and the mechanism come apart (our G3: pass on something the answer was not fitted to).

source: Taylor (2020) Folk physics for crows? (stone dropping and weight)
finding: Second line of crow evidence with the same pattern. Crows drop stones onto a platform after beak-pushing experience. In Neilands et al. (2016) they showed no preference for heavy over light objects of two colours, so they were aiming for contact, not enough force.
numbers: No preference for heavy objects shown by any crow that solved the task (Neilands 2016, as summarised).
quote: These crows can reason causally about observable features but do not make deeper inferences about unobservable causal mechanisms
limits: Summary of a prior study, not the original data.
agent_relevance: A solution that works can come from a cheaper rule (contact) than the one we credit (force). Test the cheaper rule directly before crediting the richer one.

source: Taylor (2020) Folk physics for crows? (cautions on task design)
finding: Same species looked weak or strong depending on the paradigm. Apes did better on the trap-tube when pulling with a tool than pushing (Mulcahy and Call 2006). Crows could infer object weight from watching it move in a breeze (Jelbert 2019). Crows pre-planned metatool solutions (Gruber 2019) though earlier string tests suggested they could not simulate.
numbers: No single effect size; four contrasting paradigms cited.
quote: it seems too early to interpret this pattern of results as evidence that such reasoning is beyond the capacity of the NC crow mind
limits: Review; cites others' numbers. Proposes a graded ladder of tests (hidden object, hidden mechanism, unobservable mechanism).
agent_relevance: A failure is evidence about the test as much as about the mind. Before we write 'the model cannot do X', rerun X in at least one differently built task.

source: Mecattaf et al. (2024) A little less conversation, a little more action, please (LLMs in Animal-AI)
finding: First embodied test of LLMs on Animal-AI Testbed tasks that copy animal experiments, incl. tool use and cause-effect levels. Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro, zero fine-tuning, ReAct prompt. Children beat all three on every level; LLMs never beat the top 10 Animal-AI Olympics entrants.
numbers: 3 models x 40 tasks (4 per level, 10 levels) x 3 runs each; 59 children aged 6-10 did the same 40 tasks. LLMs got some Level 1-2 tasks, sporadic wins at levels 5, 6, 8; near floor elsewhere. Exact percentages only in a figure.
quote: The children perform convincingly better than the LLM agents across all levels
limits: Floor effects at hard levels. Control scheme (action scripts, one 512x512 image per turn, max 30 action scripts) may dominate the cognitive demand. Temperature 0 but outputs still varied.
agent_relevance: Animal paradigms can be run on a language-model agent directly. But a poor score may be an interface failure, so log whether the failure is perception, control or reasoning.

source: Mecattaf et al. (2024) LLMs in Animal-AI (in-context example experiment)
finding: Giving each model a worked 'tutorial' success example did not help overall. Claude was slightly worse on Level 1 and better on Level 2. Gemini had no effect or got worse on Levels 2-3. GPT rose on Levels 2 and 3, reaching the competition upper quartile and the children's lower range on Level 3.
numbers: Experiment 2 reused the Experiment 1 setup; effect described as no notable difference overall; sample is 12 trials per level.
quote: we did not observe a notable difference in performance when providing the LLMs with the 'expert example'
limits: Small n per level, no significance tests reported in the text.
agent_relevance: A demonstration prompt is not a reliable fix for physical-reasoning gaps. Keep G7: keep a scaffold element only if it wins at equal tokens.

source: Voudouris et al. (2023) The Animal-AI Environment: a virtual laboratory for comparative cognition and AI research
finding: Platform and 900-task Testbed (spatial, memory, numerosity, tool use) built from animal studies. Causal Reasoning, Object Permanence and Numerosity levels were hard for every agent, including children. Dreamer-v3 would have placed 25th in the 2019 competition; PPO was at chance.
numbers: Odds of passing vs random agent: children 47x, competition winners ironbar and Trrrrr 19x, Dreamer-v3 6x; PPO not above chance.
quote: Three levels (Causal Reasoning, Object Permanence and Working Memory, and Numerosity and Advanced Preferences) pose difficulty for all agents
limits: Reinforcement-learning agents, not LLMs; shown as the older computational comparison class for animal-style tests.
agent_relevance: Older AI systems built for these paradigms also stall on the cause-effect levels. The test itself is hard, so low scores are not a verdict on language models alone.

source: Schulze Buschoff et al. (2023/2025) Visual cognition in multimodal large language models
finding: Five vision LLMs on classic cognitive tasks. No model matched humans in any of intuitive physics, causal reasoning, or intuitive psychology. Claude-3 Opus was robustly above chance in two of three domains. On block-tower stability only GPT-4V and Claude-3 were slightly above chance.
numbers: Tower stability: humans 65.6% correct; GPT-4V Fisher exact one-sided p=0.028, OR 2.597; Claude-3 OR 2.016, p=0.078. GPT-4V-human regression coefficient 1.15 (R2 0.066) vs human-human 1.46 (R2 0.354).
quote: none of the models matched human-level performance in any of the domains
limits: Models of 2023-2024 vintage; prompts tuned to give models a fair chance; human data from original studies.
agent_relevance: Above-chance is not human-like. A model can match a mean score while its pattern of errors differs from people's.

source: Schulze Buschoff et al. (2023/2025) Visual cognition in MLLMs (causal Jenga and Michotte tasks)
finding: On causal judgments, models tracked humans poorly. Jenga: GPT-4V coefficient with humans 0.16 (R2 0.027) vs human-human 0.54. Michotte launching: best model Fuyu 0.26 (R2 0.067, CI includes 0); Claude-3 showed a negative relation (-0.22). Human-human 0.85.
numbers: Michotte human-human coefficient 0.85 (R2 0.556); Claude-3 -0.22 (95% CI -0.39 to -0.06).
limits: Image stimuli; 18 Michotte images; some models gave constant answers (e.g. always 50 or 100).
agent_relevance: Perceived causation (contact launching) is a direct analogue of the crow 'contact vs force' split, and models fail it. Do not credit a model with causal understanding from plausible text alone.

source: Schulze Buschoff, Voudouris et al. (2025) Testing the limits of fine-tuning for improving visual cognition in VLMs
finding: Fine-tuning on ground truth for block-tower physics and causal reasoning lifts in-domain accuracy but does not transfer to other visual styles or to the other cognitive domain. A model tuned on causal pyramids did not transfer to stability of towers even with the same visuals.
numbers: 11B models reach 0.6-0.92 accuracy on the block size they were tuned on; humans 0.72 average on causal pyramids (0.68 for 3 blocks, 0.76 for 15). Below chance on some Cubeworld tower sizes.
quote: task-specific fine-tuning does not contribute to robust human-like generalization
limits: Open VLMs of 11B scale; mixing data from both domains helped somewhat (data diversity).
agent_relevance: The strongest AI parallel to the crow two-hole result: success on the trained case, then a collapse on a near variant. Always test the near variant.

source: Schulze Buschoff, Voudouris, Demircan, Schulz (2026) Can vision language models learn intuitive physics from interaction?
finding: Reinforcement learning through a simulated block-building environment (GRPO) raised in-task accuracy but not generalisation to related tasks, and interaction gave no edge over supervised tuning.
numbers: Qwen3-VL-8B in-task test accuracy GRPO 0.943 (10,000 steps), SFT 0.969. On real tower images, accuracy GRPO 0.6/0.57/0.52/0.31 across four training conditions; SFT 0.59/0.53/0.55/0.57.
quote: models trained on one task do not reliably generalize to related tasks, even if the tasks share visual statistics and physical principles
limits: One model family; synthetic training images.
agent_relevance: Even acting in a world did not produce a general rule. Doing is not the same as having the mechanism.

source: Ballout, Jassim, Bruni (2025) Pixels to Principles: probing intuitive physics in multimodal LLMs
finding: Most open multimodal models are at or below chance on GRASP; only Qwen 2.5 VL and InternVL 2.5 exceed 53% at the largest sizes. Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking gets 53.7%. Vision encoders hold the plausibility information (probes reach 85%), but the language model fails to use it.
numbers: Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking 53.7% on GRASP; Qwen 2.5 VL (72B) 99.7% on a basic visual-understanding test; probe accuracy up to 85%. Scene-level Qwen 2.5 VL 7B 68.9% on one GRASP scene set.
limits: Video benchmarks (GRASP, IntPhys 2); larger scale alone did not fix it.
agent_relevance: The knowledge can be present in one component but unused by the reasoner. In an agent loop, pass the checked fact into the step instead of hoping the model uses it.

source: Gao et al. (2025) Do vision-language models have internal world models? (WM-ABench)
finding: Atomic world-model tests grounded in comparative psychology. 15 VLMs, 660 experiments: near-random on motion trajectories; weak on prediction. Qwen2-VL predicted drop outcomes at 95.3% and lift at 91.4% in ManiSkill, but pushing was near random and drop on Physion fell to 59.2%.
numbers: Best prediction average 47.5% (Qwen2-VL). Best transitive navigation 43.8% vs human 90.0%; best collision 40.2% vs human 84.0%; manipulation 51.3% vs 88.0%. Frontier models reach 92-100% on static size comparison.
quote: almost all models perform at near-random accuracy when distinguishing motion trajectories
limits: Simulated scenes; counterfactual controls built in. Frontier models improved on mechanistic simulation (Carla navigation 60% to 81-85%).
agent_relevance: Same split as the crows: good on the trained, visible case (drop), weak where the same mechanism shows up in a new form (push).

source: Garrido et al. (2025) Intuitive physics understanding emerges from self-supervised pretraining on natural videos
finding: Violation-of-expectation tests of intuitive physics. A video model that predicts in a learned representation space (V-JEPA) is above chance on all datasets; pixel-space prediction and multimodal LLMs reasoning through text stay near chance. Zero-shot chain of thought and longer prompts did not change MLLM results.
numbers: V-JEPA average accuracy 98% (95% CI 95-99) IntPhys, 66% (64-68) GRASP, 62% (60-63) InfLevel-lab. Training only on motion videos gave near-chance.
limits: Video, not text-only; compares architectures, not scaffolds.
agent_relevance: For physical cause-effect, adding prompt scaffolds to a text-reasoning model did nothing here. Our schema cannot be expected to repair a missing world model.

source: Storks et al. (2021/2022) Tiered Reasoning for Intuitive Physics (TRIP)
finding: Models can get the right end answer without the right physical story. Best end-task accuracy 78%, yet only up to 11% of examples had both correct physical states and the conflicting sentence identified. Fine-tuning on the end task raised accuracy and lowered verifiability.
numbers: Accuracy up to 78.3%; verifiability up to 11%; of 73.6% validation items correct, about 31.4% overall had entirely wrong supporting states/conflicts.
limits: BERT-class and RoBERTa-class models, 2021; small dataset by design.
agent_relevance: Right answer is not right reasoning (G10). Check the intermediate physical claims in code, not only the final answer.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (PNAS; arXiv 2206.14576)
finding: GPT-3 got simple blicket, intervention and counterfactual vignettes right, but failed a causal-structure task. It used the observed value for interventions (fine in common-cause), yet in the causal-chain condition it gave the same predictions as common-cause, so it did not use the stated structure. Small changes to vignettes derailed it.
numbers: 12 of 12 standard vignettes correct or human-like, 6 of 12 correct; in the intervention task GPT-3 did not reduce its prediction after B=0, neither normative nor human-like.
quote: it fails miserably in causal reasoning task
limits: GPT-3 (text-davinci); later models not tested; vignette tests are widely quoted so may be memorised.
agent_relevance: Counterpart of the two-hole test: the model gets the textbook case and misses the variant that needs the underlying structure.

source: Kosoy et al. (2022) Towards understanding how machines can learn causal overhypotheses
finding: Blicket-detector benchmark adapted from child studies. Reinforcement-learning and imitation agents generalise poorly across causal overhypotheses. GPT-3 and PaLM almost always pick the right causal structure when hypotheses are given, but GPT-3 names too many objects as blickets. PaLM two-shot only works if the examples cover the test structure. Chain-of-thought did not improve results.
numbers: Four conditions (hypotheses given or not x disjunctive or conjunctive); GPT-3 text-davinci-002 temp 0.7; PaLM temp 0.
quote: We tried adding chain-of-thought reasoning in the prompt for PaLM, but were not able to improve results
limits: Small prompt set; 2022 models; results in a table of counts, not rates.
agent_relevance: Few-shot examples help only when they already cover the test structure. A new causal structure is not rescued by more examples or by CoT.

source: Samiei et al. (2026) Human adults and LLMs as scientists: who benefits from active exploration?
finding: Active blicket task with a made-up word ('nexiom'). Active exploration improved adults on conjunctive rules. Strong LLMs (gpt-5, deepseek-reasoner) matched top humans on disjunctive rules, but on conjunctive rules most models were below average adults and explored less efficiently.
numbers: Models: gpt-5, gpt-5-mini, o4-mini, gemini-2.5-flash, deepseek-chat, deepseek-reasoner; random baseline; conjunctive-disjunctive gap persisted in models. Among average adults, 16% inferred both rule and objects wrong in the conjunctive case.
quote: Nevertheless, even strong models generally remain below top human performance in conjunctive settings.
limits: Preprint; per-model n not extracted; model accuracy read from figures.
agent_relevance: Letting a model run its own tests narrows the gap in easy structures but not in the harder conjunctive one. Supports intervention-first states in the schema, with a code-counted test budget.

source: Lampinen et al. (2023) Passive learning of active causal strategies in agents and language models
finding: Agents trained only by imitation can learn to experiment first, then use what they found, and carry this to causal links never seen in training. A 70B Chinchilla LM did this from a few-shot prompt when the shots included explanations and reasoning; performance on the held-out feature dimension was far above chance.
numbers: Few-shot: four example shots from two of three dimensions (colour, shape, texture), tested on the third; with explanations performance far above 25% chance, also with an extra surprise object. Exact rates in figures only.
limits: One 70B model, odd-one-out toy world; no tool-use or physical tasks. The no-explanation arm was read from a figure, not text.
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence to a flat 'models cannot': an experiment-then-act strategy can transfer if the prompt carries explanations. Argues for the experiment-first operator.

source: Jin et al. (2024) Can large language models infer causation from correlation? (Corr2Cause, ICLR)
finding: Pure causal inference from stated correlations is near random for 17 LLMs. Fine-tuned models reached high scores but dropped sharply under paraphrase and variable renaming.
numbers: 207,972 samples, 18.57% positive; best model BART MNLI 33.38% F1, above GPT-4; many models worse than random. Fine-tuned models fell by up to 39.29 F1 (paraphrase) and 62.30 F1 (variable refactorization); few-shot CoT did not change the picture.
limits: Formal-logic framing; later reasoning models were not in the original table.
agent_relevance: Another instance of train-case success vs variant failure; also CoT did not help. Use perturbation as the pass test (G3).

source: Kiciman, Ness, Sharma, Tan (2023/2024) Causal reasoning and large language models: opening a new frontier for causality
finding: Counter-evidence: GPT-3.5/4 do well on text-based causal tasks. Pairwise causal discovery 97%, counterfactual (CRASS) 92%, necessary and sufficient cause vignettes 86%. Authors also report unpredictable failure modes.
numbers: CRASS: gpt-3.5-turbo 87.95%, gpt-4 92.44% (about 20 points above prior best). Pairwise: 97% with GPT-4 and a tuned prompt, 13 points above best covariance method.
limits: Benchmarks and vignettes may be memorised; authors test post-cutoff data (below).
agent_relevance: Models may be strong at causal talk about known domains. That does not show they hold a mechanism under novel variation.

source: Kiciman et al. (2023/2024) Causal reasoning and LLMs (robustness on post-cutoff data)
finding: Memorisation check: on a causal-direction dataset made after the training cutoff, the same prompt scored GPT-3.5-turbo 80.3% and GPT-4 98.5%.
numbers: 80.3% (GPT-3.5-turbo) and 98.5% (GPT-4) on a new dataset.
limits: Data novel in date, not necessarily novel in structure.
agent_relevance: Memorisation alone does not explain the successes, which weakens the strongest 'parrot' claim but leaves the transfer question open.

source: Zecevic, Willig, Dhami, Kersting (2023) Causal parrots: LLMs may talk causality but are not causal (TMLR)
finding: Argues that when LLMs get causal questions right, they are reciting correlations between causal facts in text (a 'meta SCM'), not running a causal model. Theory and small empirical test; no large benchmark.
numbers: No headline figure; the claim is a conjecture (Correlation of Causal Facts).
limits: Argument paper; Kiciman et al. report successes on post-cutoff data that a pure recitation account must explain. Only abstract and setup read in detail.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation to hold in mind: correct causal answers may be retrieval. Test with novel structures, not famous ones.

source: Yang, Shirvaikar, Clivio, Falck (2024) A critical review of causal reasoning benchmarks for LLMs
finding: Many LLM causal benchmarks can be solved by retrieving domain knowledge, and many test only the lowest rung (association). Proposes criteria: interventional and counterfactual items, novel variables.
numbers: Review; no single effect size.
limits: Review, not new experiments. Only abstract and introduction read in detail.
agent_relevance: Before trusting a benchmark gain for our agent, check whether the item can be answered by recall.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or reciting? Counterfactual tasks (NAACL; arXiv 2307.02477)
finding: Eleven tasks with a default and a counterfactual rule (e.g. base-9 addition, 1-based indexing). GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude and PaLM-2 stay above random on counterfactuals but fall consistently below default. A control check confirms the model understood the new rule. 0-shot CoT usually helps but sometimes hurts; few-shot CoT with up to 16 shots narrows but does not close the gap in bases 9, 11, 16.
numbers: Gap persists across all 11 tasks; accuracy gain plateaus toward 16 shots.
quote: performance substantially and consistently degrades compared to the default conditions
limits: Tasks are not physical; counterfactual worlds may be more or less difficult than default (the authors note this).
agent_relevance: A ready method: pair every task with a counterfactual variant plus a rule-comprehension control. Use it to find where our scaffold's gains are narrow.

source: Tian et al. (2024/2025) MacGyver: are LLMs creative problem solvers?
finding: 1,683 problems that need unconventional tool use (about 78% solvable). Most LLMs succeed 35-42%; a random person gets 65.1%. GPT-4's top error is wrong tool use (42.4% of its errors), followed by not achieving the goal (17.7%). Step-wise self-reflection (check each step for physical feasibility) helped GPT-4, but did not reduce infeasible answers for Llama 2.
numbers: LLMs 35-42% vs humans 65.1%; GPT-4 error mix 42.4% wrong tool usage, 17.7% goal not achieved; GPT-4 and PaLM2 very poor at flagging unsolvable problems.
limits: Text problems; human data on a 323-problem subset; solvability flags made by annotators.
agent_relevance: Direct analogue of a tool-affordance test. Gives a method already used in an LLM loop: a feasibility-check pass over each step. It only helped the strong model.

source: Ullman (2023) Large language models fail on trivial alterations to theory-of-mind tasks
finding: Small changes that keep the theory-of-mind logic flip a claimed LLM success into failure. Argues the default stance should be sceptical and that outlying failures outweigh average success.
quote: the zero-hypothesis for model evaluation in intuitive psychology should be skeptical
limits: Only abstract and introduction read this session; no numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as the two-hole tube: a trivial rearrangement is the cheapest test of whether a mechanism is held.

source: Shapira et al. (2024) Clever Hans or neural theory of mind? Stress testing social reasoning in LLMs
finding: Six theory-of-mind tasks. Some near-saturated (TriangleCOPA 96% by flan-t5-xxl), others hard; adversarial versions expose shallow heuristics. On ToMi, GPT-3.5 gets 81% overall but 46% on false-belief questions. GPT-4 SocialIQa 79% overall, 74.5% on 'others'.
numbers: Adv-CSFB 'other person' accuracy fell from 93.8% (davinci-002) to 68.8% (GPT-4); 'inon' from 71.4% to 0%. Probing method changed GPT-4 SocialIQa accuracy by 7 points (multiple choice vs CoT).
limits: Some of the reported drops come from specific categories with few items.
agent_relevance: Clever Hans lens: headline accuracy hides cue use. Break the cue (adversarial item) and score the subset.
